query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Oxidation resistance and the long‐term integrity of multiprincipal‐element high‐temperature alloys are governed by the differential oxidizability of their constituent elements. In these alloys, elements with higher redox potentials (and generally smaller atomic sizes) preferentially oxidize to form a nanocrystalline, adherent surface oxide. This protective scale, mediated by dynamically amorphized grain boundary regions, reduces further oxygen ingress and thus preserves the alloy’s structural integrity under harsh conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic, single‐phase multiprincipal‐element alloy (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn) with a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by enriching or depleting one or more elements with high redox potential (for example, increasing Cr content) and subject the samples to identical high-temperature, oxygen-controlled environments.
generation.conditions: Testing performed at high temperatures (approximately 600–800 °C) under controlled oxygen partial pressures and under similar mechanical loading conditions to assess both oxidation kinetics and mechanical integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a nanocrystalline, protective oxide film at the alloy’s surface, with its structure influenced by dynamically altered grain boundaries (i.e., dynamic amorphization), which jointly mediate the barrier properties of the oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: Due to differences in atomic size and redox potential, elements with higher redox potentials oxidize first. This rapid formation of stable oxides creates a continuous, nanocrystalline barrier that limits oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy. The protective effect is enhanced by dynamic grain boundary processes (as seen in inverse Hall-Petch behavior) which contribute to stress accommodation and maintain the integrity of the interface between the oxide scale and the substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys enriched in high redox potential elements will form thinner, more adherent, and compositionally stable oxide layers, thereby exhibiting slower oxidation kinetics and better retention of mechanical properties (e.g., creep and wear resistance) relative to the equiatomic baseline.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, which is expected to show a more typical oxide growth profile and correspondingly less optimized mechanical retention under high-temperature oxidation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold for high-temperature applications in the range of approximately 600–800 °C under moderate mechanical loads. It may not extend to regimes where phase transformations or extensive microstructural coarsening occur, which could alter oxidation kinetics and mechanical responses.
generation.uncertainty: The relative quantitative contributions of atomic size effects versus redox potential in controlling oxide morphology, as well as potential synergistic or antagonistic effects from minor alloying elements, remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the standard equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy (baseline) and a second set modified to have a >10% enrichment of a high redox potential element (e.g., Cr). Expose both sets to identical high-temperature and oxygen-controlled conditions. Use in-situ atom probe tomography, TEM, and X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy to characterize the oxide layer formation and nanostructure at the surface. Complement these with nanoindentation and wear tests to assess mechanical integrity.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and morphology (via TEM, high-resolution imaging)
Chemical composition of the oxide scale (using atom probe tomography and X-ray absorption spectroscopy)
Grain size and nanocrystalline structure analysis near the surface
Mechanical property retention (nanoindentation creep properties, wear resistance)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy enriched with high redox potential elements does not form a significantly thinner, more adherent, and compositionally stable oxide layer and does not exhibit improved mechanical performance relative to the equiatomic baseline, then the hypothesis that differential elemental oxidizability governs oxidation resistance and material integrity is falsified.

Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys

Abstract: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
